s: The southern Libyan desert is barren, dry, and without water, resembling a vast featureless sea. It contains long stretches of sand, almost no plants or animals, and many venomous serpents.

s: Sand forms extensive heaps across the inland desert and makes the Cerestes difficult to see because they are the same color as the ground. People may step on them unknowingly and risk losing their lives.

l: serpents, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now given an account of these countries, it will well agree
s: The desert contains serpents of many shapes and sizes, whose bites are described as mortal. They are especially numerous in the barren sandy regions and are reported to have once devastated much of Egypt.

l: Cerestes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now given an account of these countries, it will well agree
s: Cerestes are serpents whose bites are mortal. Because they resemble the sand in color, they are difficult to distinguish from the ground and may be stepped on accidentally.

l: air apparitions, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now given an account of these countries, it will well agree
s: Air apparitions appear in the deserts and near the Syrtes, especially during calm weather, in shapes resembling large living creatures. Some seem to stand, move, fly, or pursue people, frightening strangers and sometimes causing them to feel cold and tremble.

l: air, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having now given an account of these countries, it will well agree
s: The air in the dry region is said to become thick because few vapors arise to produce winds. According to the natural philosophers cited, it can condense into various shapes, drift and consolidate, fall to the ground, adhere to living bodies, and produce the movements and chilling effects attributed to the apparitions.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: The unit describes the ancient Amazons of Africa, who lived under female rule and became powerful warriors under their queen Merina. They conquered parts of Africa and Asia, including the Atlantides, but fought the Gorgons and were eventually extirpated along with them by Hercules. Perseus later conquered the Gorgons under Medusa, while an earthquake caused the Tritonis morass to disappear. The account also connects the Amazons with Atlas and the Atlantides and describes their eventual defeat by Thracian invaders.

l: Amazons of Africa, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: The Amazons of Africa were an ancient nation governed by women who managed warfare, magistracies, and public offices, while men cared for household affairs. Under Merina, they conquered the Atlantides, fought the Gorgons, overran parts of Africa and Asia, built several cities, and possessed islands including Lesbos. After repeated defeats by Mompsus and Sipylus, the surviving Amazons withdrew into Libya, and Hercules later extirpated them.

l: Gorgons, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: The Gorgons were an African nation of courageous and powerful women who were enemies of the Amazons and frequently troubled the Atlantides. Merina defeated them and captured three thousand of them, but they later remained powerful until Medusa's reign, when Perseus conquered them. Hercules eventually extirpated the Gorgons.

l: Perseus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: Perseus made war against the Gorgons and conquered them during the reign of Medusa.

l: Hercules, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: Hercules extirpated both the Gorgons and the Amazons when he traveled into the western parts and erected a pillar in Africa. He could not tolerate a nation being governed by women because he sought renown throughout the world.

l: Tritonis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: Tritonis was a morass near the ocean and the island of Hisperia, bordered by Ethiopia and associated with the river Triton. The Amazons built the city of Chersonesus in it, but an earthquake later opened the tract toward the ocean and swallowed up the entire morass.

l: Mount Atlas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: Atlas was the name the Grecians gave to the greatest mountain in the region bordering the Tritonis morass and extending to the ocean. The Amazons attacked the people living upon Mount Atlas, who possessed a rich country with many cities.

l: Atlantides, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: The Atlantides inhabited a rich country near Mount Atlas and were initially defeated by Merina and the Amazons. After the destruction of Cercene, they submitted, gave up their cities, and formed a league with Merina, who received them into her favor. They presented Merina with rich gifts and honored her.

l: Merina, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, CHAP. IV.
s: Merina was queen of the Amazons and led an army of thirty thousand foot soldiers and two thousand horse. She conquered the Atlantides, fought the Gorgons, overran parts of Africa and Asia, founded cities, and consecrated Samothracia to the mother of the gods after surviving a storm. She was later killed in battle against Mompsus and Sipylus and was succeeded in defeat by the remaining Amazons.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And now, since we have made mention of the Atlantides, we judge
s: The unit reports what the Atlantides and Phrygians say about the genealogy of the gods and the origins of their worship. Uranus and Titea are presented as the parents of the Titans, including Basilea, Hyperion, and other divine ancestors. It recounts the deaths and deification of Helios and Selene, the history of Cybele and Atys, and the contest between Marsyas and Apollo. It also describes the Phrygian worship of Cybele and the division of the kingdom between Atlas and Saturn after Hyperion's death.

l: Atlantides, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And now, since we have made mention of the Atlantides, we judge
s: The Atlantides are said to inhabit a rich country bordering the ocean and to excel their neighbors in civilized reception and entertainment of strangers. They report an account of the genealogy of the gods, including the history of Uranus, Titea, Basilea, Hyperion, Cybele, and the other figures described here.

l: genealogy of the gods, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And now, since we have made mention of the Atlantides, we judge
s: The reported genealogy begins with Uranus and Titea, whose children include the Titans, Basilea, and Rhea. It further traces the divine status of Helios, Selene, and Cybele.

l: gods, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And now, since we have made mention of the Atlantides, we judge
s: The gods are said to have been born among the Atlantides, according to their report. Several human rulers and benefactors, including Uranus, Titea, Helios, Selene, and Cybele, are said to have been honored as gods after their deaths or notable deeds.

l: Uranus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And now, since we have made mention of the Atlantides, we judge
s: Uranus is described as the first king of the Atlantides, who settled wandering people in towns and cities and taught them to use and store the fruits of the earth. He practiced astrology, measured years and months by the sun and moon, divided days into hours, and was honored as a god after his death; the starry heaven was named after him.

l: Terra, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And now, since we have made mention of the Atlantides, we judge
s: Titea was the mother of eighteen of Uranus's children, who were collectively called Titans. Because of her wisdom and beneficence, she was reputed a goddess after her death and was called Terra.

l: Titans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And now, since we have made mention of the Atlantides, we judge
s: The Titans were the eighteen children of Uranus and Titea, collectively named after their mother. They were later expected to execute revenge upon the malefactor responsible for the deaths of Hyperion and Helios.

l: Basilea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And now, since we have made mention of the Atlantides, we judge
s: Basilea was the eldest and most prudent daughter of Uranus and Titea. She raised her brothers with maternal care, became known as the Great Mother, and was elected queen after her father's death while still a virgin.

l: Hyperion, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And now, since we have made mention of the Atlantides, we judge
s: Hyperion was Basilea's brother and husband, whom she loved dearly. Their brothers conspired against him because of envy and fear that he would take the kingdom entirely, and they assassinated him.

l: the sun, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And now, since we have made mention of the Atlantides, we judge
s: Helios was the son of Basilea and Hyperion and the brother of Selene. He was drowned in Eridanus as a tender infant, after which he was deified and his name was transferred to the sun.

l: Selene, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And now, since we have made mention of the Atlantides, we judge
s: Selene was the daughter of Basilea and Hyperion and passionately loved her brother Helios. After learning of his death, she threw herself from the housetop, and her name was later transferred to the moon.

l: Cybele, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And now, since we have made mention of the Atlantides, we judge
s: Cybele is described as a goddess also called the Mother of the Mountains. She was abandoned on Mount Cybelus, was nourished by leopards and other wild beasts, invented the multi-reed pipe, timbrel, and cymbal, and learned methods of treating diseases in children and cattle. After Atys and her nurses were killed, she became mad and wandered through the country; the Phrygians later worshiped her as a goddess.

l: Phrygia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And now, since we have made mention of the Atlantides, we judge
s: Phrygia is said to be the birthplace of Cybele. Its inhabitants report that Mæones ruled Phrygia and Lydia, that Cybele was exposed on Mount Cybelus, and that the Phrygians later established her worship at Pessinunte.

l: Marsyas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And now, since we have made mention of the Atlantides, we judge
s: Marsyas was a Phrygian associated with Cybele and described as ingenious and remarkably chaste. He followed Cybele during her madness and contested Apollo in music, but Apollo defeated him and flayed him alive.

l: Atys (Papas), The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And now, since we have made mention of the Atlantides, we judge
s: Atys, later called Papas, was a young native whom Cybele loved and accompanied, becoming pregnant by him. Cybele's father ordered Atys and her nurses to be killed after learning of the pregnancy, and the bodies were left without burial.

l: Apollo, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And now, since we have made mention of the Atlantides, we judge
s: Apollo was highly esteemed for playing the harp, which Mercury had invented. He defeated Marsyas in a musical contest, flayed him alive in anger, later regretted the act, broke the strings of his harp, and consecrated both the harp and hautboy to Bacchus.

l: Phrygians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And now, since we have made mention of the Atlantides, we judge
s: The Phrygians sought an oracle during a plague and famine and were instructed to bury Atys and adore Cybele as a goddess. Unable to find Atys's body, they made a statue for him and performed funeral ceremonies, while establishing yearly sacrifices and worship for Cybele.

l: Atlas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And now, since we have made mention of the Atlantides, we judge
s: Atlas was one of the most renowned children of Coelus after Hyperion's death. The country bordering the ocean fell to him by lot, and he called its people after himself.

l: Saturn, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And now, since we have made mention of the Atlantides, we judge
s: Saturn was one of the most renowned children of Coelus after Hyperion's death. He shared in the division of the kingdom among Coelus's children.

l: contest between Marsyas and Apollo, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And now, since we have made mention of the Atlantides, we judge
s: Marsyas and Apollo competed to determine who was the greater artist, with the Nysians serving as judges. Apollo ultimately won after performing with his harp and voice, and Marsyas was subsequently flayed alive.

l: worship of Cybele, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And now, since we have made mention of the Atlantides, we judge
s: The worship of Cybele began after the people believed Basilea, or the mother described in the account, was a goddess. The Phrygians later instituted sacrifices and divine rites for Cybele, built her a magnificent temple at Pessinunte with the assistance of King Midas, and placed leopards and lions beside her statue.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Atlantides, and the greatest mountain in the world Atlas, after his
s: The unit describes Atlas, the Atlantides, and their associations with astrology, the stars, heroic ancestry, and the Pleiades. It recounts Saturn’s rule over western lands and Jupiter Olympus’s succession, conquests, and divine honors. It then presents several accounts of Bacchus, including interpretations of him as wine, as the discoverer of viticulture and agriculture, and as the son of Jupiter and Semele who spread his rites throughout the world. The text also explains the natural and mythological origins and uses of the vine and wine.

l: Atlas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Atlantides, and the greatest mountain in the world Atlas, after his
s: Atlas was said to have been an excellent astrologer and the first to discover knowledge of the sphere, which led to the belief that he carried the world upon his shoulders. He gave his name to the greatest mountain in the world and had many sons, including Hesperus, as well as seven daughters called the Atlantides.

l: Atlantides, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Atlantides, and the greatest mountain in the world Atlas, after his
s: The Atlantides were Atlas’s seven daughters: Maia, Electra, Taygeta, Asterope, Merope, Halcyone, and Celseno. They bore sons by heroic princes and gods, becoming ancestors of nations and cities; after their deaths they were worshipped as goddesses and placed among the stars as the Pleiades. Nymphs were also commonly called Atlantides because nympha was a general term for women in that country.

l: Saturn, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Atlantides, and the greatest mountain in the world Atlas, after his
s: Saturn, Atlas’s brother, was described as profane and covetous. He married his sister Rhea and was said to have ruled Sicily, Africa, Italy, and the western parts of the world, securing his dominion with garrisons and forts; the high mounts in western Sicily were consequently called Cronia.

l: Jupiter Triphylius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Atlantides, and the greatest mountain in the world Atlas, after his
s: Jupiter, the son of Saturn, was said to have treated his subjects justly and courteously and was therefore called Father. He succeeded Saturn, defeated him in battle with the aid of the Titans’ opposition, conquered the world, punished the impious, and benefited mankind. After his death he was placed in the highest heavens and worshipped as a god and supreme lord of the earth, receiving the name Zena from his instruction of men in proper living.

l: Bacchus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Atlantides, and the greatest mountain in the world Atlas, after his
s: The text gives several accounts of Bacchus, including one in which he is identified with wine and others in which there were one or three human Bacchuses. One Bacchus was said to have discovered the vine and the uses of wine, another to have taught ploughing with oxen and other agricultural arts, and a third to have been born at Thebes to Jupiter and Semele. The last of these travelled through the world with armed women, taught rites and ceremonies, promoted festivals, peace, and concord, and punished opponents including Pentheus, Myrrhanus, and Lycurgus.

l: wine, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Atlantides, and the greatest mountain in the world Atlas, after his
s: Wine is treated by some naturalists as the substance represented by Bacchus. It was said to come from grapes pressed from the vine, and boiling wine was interpreted as a process intended to make it stronger and more fragrant.

l: vine, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Atlantides, and the greatest mountain in the world Atlas, after his
s: The vine was said to have been naturally produced by the earth and not originally planted or discovered by anyone, as shown by wild vines that bore grapes without cultivation. In mythological interpretations, its growth, fruiting, destruction, pruning, and renewed flourishing were represented through the births, dismemberment, boiling, and revival of Bacchus.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The poet in his hymns confirms what we have before declared^
s: The unit discusses competing accounts of Bacchus’s birthplace and distinguishes three Bacchuses, focusing chiefly on the first, whom the Libyans say was the son of Ammon and Amalthaea and was raised at Nysa. It recounts the first Bacchus’s education, inventions, wars against Saturn and the Titans, worldwide benefactions, and eventual worship as a god. It also describes the roles of Rhea, Saturn, Jupiter, Aristaeus, Minerva, the Amazons, and others in these events. Finally, it identifies the second Bacchus as the son of Jupiter and Io and the third as the son of Jupiter and Semele.

l: Bacchus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The poet in his hymns confirms what we have before declared^
s: Bacchus is associated with several proposed birthplaces, including Nysa, Thebes, and other locations. The Libyans describe a first Bacchus, son of Ammon and Amalthaea, who was raised at Nysa, invented or taught the use of wine and cultivation, fought Saturn and the Titans, benefited mankind, and was worshipped as a god; the text also identifies a second Bacchus as the son of Jupiter and Io and a third as the son of Jupiter and Semele.

l: Nysa, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The poet in his hymns confirms what we have before declared^
s: Nysa is described as an island city surrounded by the river Triton and accessible through the Nysian gates. It is portrayed as a fertile, beautiful, and healthful place of meadows, gardens, orchards, streams, caves, flowers, trees, and birds, where Bacchus was raised and instructed.

l: Jupiter, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The poet in his hymns confirms what we have before declared^
s: Jupiter was the son of Saturn and Rhea and was later advanced to positions of honor by Dionysius. He became king after receiving instruction from Olympus, was made king of Egypt, and later became lord of the universe; the text also names him as the father of the second Bacchus by Io and of the third Bacchus by Semele.

l: Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The poet in his hymns confirms what we have before declared^
s: Egypt was ruled by Jupiter after Dionysius invaded it and appointed him king. Dionysius was said to have taught the Egyptians how to plant vines and preserve wine, apples, and other fruits.

l: Africans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The poet in his hymns confirms what we have before declared^
s: The Africans living on the sea-coasts claim that Bacchus was born among them and that his reported deeds occurred there. They cite surviving marks and signs, support their account through ancient and modern writers, and later joined Dionysius as allies against the Titans.

l: Libya, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The poet in his hymns confirms what we have before declared^
s: Libya is presented as the region in which Ammon ruled and where the first Bacchus carried out several exploits. Dionysius traveled through Libya, gained Libyan support, and was said to have improved its lands and benefited its inhabitants.

l: Ammon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The poet in his hymns confirms what we have before declared^
s: Ammon was a king in Libya who married Rhea and fathered Bacchus by Amalthaea. He sent the child to Nysa for protection, was defeated and driven from his kingdom by Saturn and the Titans, later ruled Crete with Geta, and was worshipped as a god after Dionysius built a city and temple in his honor.

l: Rhea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The poet in his hymns confirms what we have before declared^
s: Rhea was the daughter of Coelus and sister of Saturn and the other Titans, and she married Ammon. Jealous of Amalthaea’s child, she tried to seize Dionysius; she later joined Saturn against Ammon, married Saturn, and was eventually captured but pardoned by Dionysius, whom she loved as her own son.

l: Saturn, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The poet in his hymns confirms what we have before declared^
s: Saturn married Rhea and, encouraged by her, joined the Titans in making war on Ammon. He defeated Ammon, ruled cruelly, fought Dionysius, was wounded and defeated, and was later pardoned and treated as a parent by Dionysius, although the text says Saturn’s affection was deceitful.

l: Amalthaea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The poet in his hymns confirms what we have before declared^
s: Amalthaea was a beautiful virgin whom Ammon met in the Ceraunean mountains and by whom he fathered a son who became famous for strength and beauty. She became queen of a neighboring fertile region called Amalthaea’s Horn, and her child was sent away to Nysa because Ammon feared Rhea’s jealousy.

l: Aristaeus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The poet in his hymns confirms what we have before declared^
s: Aristaeus was one of Nysa’s sisters’ associates and was appointed to tutor the child Dionysius. He is described as prudent, honest, and learned, and he was said to have first offered sacrifices to Dionysius as a god.

l: Minerva, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The poet in his hymns confirms what we have before declared^
s: Minerva was appointed guardian of Dionysius at Nysa. She was described as a wise and courageous virgin warrior who killed the fire-breathing monster Aegides, assisted in destroying the giants, and commanded the women in Dionysius’s army.

l: Titans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The poet in his hymns confirms what we have before declared^
s: The Titans joined Saturn in attacking Ammon and later fought Dionysius with forces in Libya and Crete. Dionysius defeated them, initially threatened them with death, then pardoned them; they chose to serve him, and the text later says that all the Titans were destroyed.

l: Crete, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The poet in his hymns confirms what we have before declared^
s: Ammon fled to Crete after being driven from his kingdom and married Geta, one of the daughters of the ruling Curetes, gaining the island’s sovereignty. Crete was later the site of a war between the Titans and the forces supporting Ammon, in which Dionysius and his allies were victorious.

l: Amazons, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The poet in his hymns confirms what we have before declared^
s: The Amazons were described as valiant warriors and virgins who had brought parts of the world under their dominion. They joined Dionysius against the Titans, chiefly because of their association with Minerva, and their women were commanded by Minerva in the battle.

l: Semele, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The poet in his hymns confirms what we have before declared^
s: Semele was the mother of the third Bacchus, who was described as the son of Jupiter and Semele. The text treats this Bacchus as a later figure who rivaled the earlier Bacchuses and traveled through the world.

l: wine, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The poet in his hymns confirms what we have before declared^
s: Wine was used by Dionysius as a sacred pledge when he pardoned the Titans and required them to swear loyalty. The pouring out and drinking of wine was said to have originated the practice by which truces and wartime leagues were called libations, and Dionysius was credited with teaching its production and use.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS- / BOOK IV.
s: Diodorus Siculus explains that he will treat the antiquities of the Grecians, including their gods, demi-gods, famous men, and beneficial inventions. He begins with Dionysius, also called Bacchus, whom the Greeks say discovered wine and wine-making, civilized many nations, and led an expedition to India. The account also describes Cadmus, Semele, Jupiter, Priapus, Hermaphroditus, and the Muses before turning to Hercules and the difficulty of relating his extraordinary labours. Diodorus argues that ancient traditions should not be rejected merely because their marvels seem incredible.

l: Diodorus Siculus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS- / BOOK IV.
s: Diodorus Siculus states that ancient history is difficult to compile because accounts, genealogies, and chronologies often differ. He resolves to relate the antiquities of the Grecians and begins with Dionysius because he considers him the most ancient and the greatest benefactor to mankind.

l: Greeks, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS- / BOOK IV.
s: The Greeks report that Dionysius was the son of Jupiter and Semele, was brought up at Nysa, discovered wine and wine-making, and civilized many nations. They also celebrate festivals and sacrifices in his honour.

l: Dionysius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS- / BOOK IV.
s: Dionysius is presented as a god who discovered wine, taught people to plant the vine, made barley drink for regions unsuitable for vines, and civilized many nations. The text distinguishes an older Dionysius, the son of Jupiter and Proserpina, from the later Dionysius, the son of Semele, although both were credited with similar actions.

l: Bacchus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS- / BOOK IV.
s: Bacchus is another name for Dionysius, who led men and women on expeditions, punished impious people, instituted festivals, plays, theatres, and music-schools, and was honoured for the benefits he brought to mankind. He is associated with the Muses, satyrs, Silenus, wine, and the Indian expedition.

l: wine, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS- / BOOK IV.
s: Wine is described as a pleasant and strengthening drink discovered by Dionysius. Pure wine was believed to cause madness, while wine mixed with water was said to cheer and refresh the spirits and cure intoxication.

l: Cadmus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS- / BOOK IV.
s: Cadmus, the son of Agenor, was sent from Phoenicia to seek Europa and was commanded not to return without her. After failing to find her, he came to Boeotia, built Thebes by command of an oracle, and married Hermione, by whom he had Semele and other children.

l: Semele, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS- / BOOK IV.
s: Semele, the daughter of Cadmus and Hermione, was loved by Jupiter and became pregnant by him. At her request Jupiter appeared in his divine majesty, and the lightning consumed her before she could give birth; Jupiter then took the infant and entrusted him to Mercury.

l: Jupiter, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS- / BOOK IV.
s: Jupiter loved Semele and fathered Dionysius by her. When he appeared to her in thunder and lightning at her request, Semele was consumed by the flames, after which Jupiter arranged for the infant to be taken to Nysa.

l: India, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS- / BOOK IV.
s: India is the destination of Dionysius's three-year expedition. He returned from India with rich spoils and was said to have been the first to triumph while mounted on an Indian elephant.

l: Muses, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS- / BOOK IV.
s: The Muses are generally said to be the nine daughters of Jupiter and Mnemosyne, although some writers give them a different parentage or number. They are associated with poetry, harmony, dancing, singing, astrology, and other liberal arts, and are said to attend Dionysius on his expeditions.

l: Hercules, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS- / BOOK IV.
s: Hercules is introduced as a hero whose actions exceeded those of all others recorded in the world. Diodorus says that his deeds are difficult to relate because their greatness and strangeness may seem incredible, but he will report them according to ancient poets and mythologists.

l: India expedition, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS- / BOOK IV.
s: The India expedition lasted three whole years and was led by Dionysius. His return with spoils and an Indian elephant was commemorated by the Trieterica and other festivals held every third year.

l: twelve labours of Hercules, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS- / BOOK IV.
s: Hercules' labours are described as extraordinarily numerous and difficult to match in greatness. Diodorus warns that he may omit some deeds so that the whole account will not be rejected as fabulous.

l: antiquities of the Grecians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, DIODORUS SICULUS- / BOOK IV.
s: The antiquities of the Grecians are the subject of this book. They include accounts of gods, demi-gods, famous warriors, inventors of beneficial practices, and law-makers from the most ancient times.

s: History preserves the praises of gods, demi-gods, and other worthy people for successive generations. Diodorus says that history suffers when ancient accounts are judged by standards suited only to recent events, and he urges readers not to examine old stories too critically.

s: Dionysius is credited with discovering the use of wine and teaching people how to plant the vine. He also taught the making of a barley drink called Zythus in countries where vines could not be grown.

s: The unit recounts the birth, upbringing, and early exploits of Hercules, son of Jupiter and Alcmena, including Juno's attempts to hinder him. Hercules frees Thebes from the tribute imposed by Erginus, marries Megara, and is later compelled by Eurystheus to undertake twelve labours. He kills the Nemean lion, destroys the Hydra of Lerna, captures the Erymanthian boar, defeats the centaurs, and completes several further tasks. He also assists the gods against the giants, frees Prometheus, and defeats the Amazons to obtain Hippolyta's belt.

l: Jupiter Triphylius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Perseus (they say) was the son of Jupiter by Danae, the daughter
s: Jupiter fathers Hercules with Alcmena after deceiving her by taking the shape of Amphitryon, and he lengthens the night threefold. He declares that the child born that day will be king of the Persians, later arranges that Hercules may gain immortality through twelve labours, and commands him to obey Eurystheus.

l: Alcmena, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Perseus (they say) was the son of Jupiter by Danae, the daughter
s: Alcmena bears Hercules by Jupiter, who approaches her in the shape of Amphitryon. Fearing Juno's jealousy, she exposes the child in a place later called Hercules's Field, though the child is subsequently returned to her to be nursed.

l: Hercules, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Perseus (they say) was the son of Jupiter by Danae, the daughter
s: Hercules is presented as exceptionally strong and virtuous from birth. He strangles two serpents sent by Juno, frees Thebes from Erginus, marries Megara, kills his children during a fit of madness, and then undertakes the labours imposed by Eurystheus. He performs numerous feats, including killing the Nemean lion and Hydra, defeating the centaurs, assisting the gods against the giants, freeing Prometheus, and defeating the Amazons.

l: Juno, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Perseus (they say) was the son of Jupiter by Danae, the daughter
s: Juno delays Alcmena's delivery so that Eurystheus is born first and can become king according to Jupiter's declaration. She later sends two serpents to kill Hercules, but he strangles them, and she strikes him with madness after he is ordered to serve Eurystheus.

l: Eurystheus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Perseus (they say) was the son of Jupiter by Danae, the daughter
s: Eurystheus is brought forth before his full time through Juno's intervention and becomes king. He commands Hercules to perform twelve labours, including killing the Nemean lion, and is terrified when Hercules brings him the Erymanthian boar.

l: Nemean lion, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Perseus (they say) was the son of Jupiter by Danae, the daughter
s: The Nemean lion is a monstrous beast whose hide cannot be pierced or wounded by weapons or stones. Hercules traps it in its den, strangles it with his arms, and thereafter wears its skin as protection.

l: Hydra of Lerna, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Perseus (they say) was the son of Jupiter by Danae, the daughter
s: The Hydra of Lerna has a hundred necks and serpent heads, with two heads growing whenever one is cut off. Hercules has Iolaus burn the severed parts to stop them from regenerating, kills the monster, and dips his arrows in its gall so that their wounds cannot be healed.

l: centaurs, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Perseus (they say) was the son of Jupiter by Danae, the daughter
s: The centaurs attack Hercules after Pholus opens a wine jar, and they fight with trees, stones, firebrands, and axes. Hercules defeats them despite their physical advantages and the rain sent by their mother Nephele, killing many and putting the rest to flight.

l: Amazons, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Perseus (they say) was the son of Jupiter by Danae, the daughter
s: The Amazons refuse Hercules's demand for Hippolyta's belt, so he attacks them near Themiscyra at the mouth of the Thermodon. He kills many of their leading warriors, defeats their queen Melanippe, forces the remainder to flee, and destroys their nation; he gives Antiope to Theseus and releases Melanippe after taking her belt.

l: Thebes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Perseus (they say) was the son of Jupiter by Danae, the daughter
s: Thebes is ruled by Creon while suffering under the tribute imposed by Erginus, king of the Minyans. Hercules arms the young men, kills Erginus, destroys the Minyan power, and is rewarded by Creon with Megara and responsibility for the city.

l: twelve labours of Hercules, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Perseus (they say) was the son of Jupiter by Danae, the daughter
s: The twelve labours are imposed on Hercules by Eurystheus after the oracle at Delphi declares that he must perform them to receive immortality. In this unit they include killing the Nemean lion and Hydra of Lerna, capturing the Erymanthian boar and the golden-horned hind, driving away the Stymphalian birds, cleansing Augeas's stable, bringing the Cretan bull, obtaining Diomedes's mares, and taking Hippolyta's belt; the text also associates the Erymanthian task with the defeat of the centaurs and later mentions the golden fleece expedition.

s: Eurystheus imposed upon Hercules the tenth labour of driving away the oxen of Gerion from Iberia. Hercules assembled a fleet and army, defeated the sons of Chrysaor, and took the herds. He then travelled through Libya, Iberia, Gaul, Italy, and Sicily, where he performed various feats, founded or improved places, and received honours and sacrifices.

l: Hercules, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, After this, a tenth labour was imposed upon him by Em7stheii%
s: Hercules undertook the tenth labour imposed by Eurystheus and assembled a fleet and army for the expedition to Iberia. He defeated the sons of Chrysaor, took the oxen of Gerion, and travelled through Libya, Iberia, Gaul, Italy, and Sicily, where he destroyed wild beasts and tyrants, improved lands and roads, performed various works, and received honours and sacrifices.

s: Eurystheus imposed upon Hercules the task of driving away the oxen of Gerion. He chose it because he believed the expedition was too great for Hercules to accomplish.

l: the tenth labour of Hercules, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, After this, a tenth labour was imposed upon him by Em7stheii%
s: The tenth labour was to drive away the oxen of Gerion, which pastured in Iberia near the ocean. Hercules completed it after defeating the three sons of Chrysaor and taking the herds.

l: oxen of Gerion, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, After this, a tenth labour was imposed upon him by Em7stheii%
s: The oxen of Gerion pastured in Iberia near the ocean. Hercules drove them away, transported them through his expedition, and later brought them into Sicily and back into Italy.

l: Iberia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, After this, a tenth labour was imposed upon him by Em7stheii%
s: Iberia was ruled by Chrysaor, whose three sons commanded mighty armies there. Hercules defeated the sons, gained Iberia, drove away the oxen of Gerion, and later entrusted the government of the kingdom to its chief inhabitants.

l: sons of Chrysaor, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, After this, a tenth labour was imposed upon him by Em7stheii%
s: The three sons of Chrysaor were strong-bodied and renowned in martial affairs, each having a large army. Hercules challenged and slew the three generals, thereby gaining Iberia and the herds of oxen.

l: Gerion, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, After this, a tenth labour was imposed upon him by Em7stheii%
s: Gerion was one of the sons of Chrysaor and was associated with the remarkable herds of cattle taken by Hercules. Hercules later consecrated a grove to Gerion as to a demi-god, and the inhabitants worshipped him.

l: Libya, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, After this, a tenth labour was imposed upon him by Em7stheii%
s: In Libya, Hercules slew Antaeus and destroyed wild beasts. He made the country safer and more productive, and was said to have improved its fertility and purged its cities of wicked men and insolent tyrants.

l: Pillars of Hercules, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, After this, a tenth labour was imposed upon him by Em7stheii%
s: Hercules erected the Pillars of Hercules on opposite sides of the strait near the ocean, as lasting monuments of his expedition. The text also reports competing accounts that he either narrowed the passage by building up the mountains or cut a trench through joined continents.

l: Italy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, After this, a tenth labour was imposed upon him by Em7stheii%
s: Hercules entered Italy after passing through Gaul and the Alps. He travelled through Liguria, Tuscany, the region of Rome, and the maritime coasts, killed Lacinius, buried Croton, and eventually passed through Epirus into Peloponnesus.

l: Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, After this, a tenth labour was imposed upon him by Em7stheii%
s: Hercules brought the oxen into Sicily by causing them to swim across the sea and then travelled around the island. He received honours at Syracuse and among the Agyrineans, fought the Sicani, and instituted or inspired sacrifices, festivals, temples, and other sacred observances.

s: Hercules completes his tenth labour by bringing Cerberus out of hell after being initiated at Eleusis, then undertakes the labour of obtaining the golden apples or sheep of the Hesperides. The account describes Orpheus, Atlas, the Hesperides, and the Amazons, including Theseus’s defeat of the Amazons in Attica. After completing his labours, Hercules establishes a colony in Sardinia through Iolaus and the Thespiadae, serves Omphale, attacks Troy, and conducts further wars against Augeas and the rulers of Sparta. The unit ends with Hercules’s relationship to Auge, the story of Telephus, and his marriage to Deianira after the death of Meleager.

s: After Hercules finished his tenth labour, Eurystheus imposed another task upon him: bringing Cerberus out of hell. After Hercules completed his labours, Eurystheus later banished him, Alcmena, Epicle, and Iolaus from the kingdom.

l: Hercules, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having finished his tenth labour, £urystheus imposed anoAer
s: Hercules was initiated at Eleusis before entering hell, where he freed Theseus and Pirithous and brought Cerberus away. He obtained the golden apples or sheep of the Hesperides, founded a colony in Sardinia through Iolaus and the Thespiadae, served Omphale, captured Troy, and fought Augeas and Hippocoon. He later became involved with Auge and married Deianira after Meleager's death.

l: twelve labours of Hercules, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having finished his tenth labour, £urystheus imposed anoAer
s: Hercules's tenth labour was to bring Cerberus out of hell, and the last labour was to fetch the golden apples of the Hesperides. After completing all his labours, he expected, according to the oracle of Apollo, to be rewarded with immortality.

l: Cerberus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having finished his tenth labour, £urystheus imposed anoAer
s: Cerberus was the dog of hell. Hercules brought him up from the infernal regions tied in his chain and presented him to open view.

l: Orpheus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having finished his tenth labour, £urystheus imposed anoAer
s: Orpheus was the son of Oeagrus and a Thracian who excelled in music and poetry. His music was said to draw wild beasts and trees after him, and he became learned in ancient theology, divinity, sacred mysteries, music, and poetry. He descended into hell for love of his wife and persuaded Proserpine to let him take her back.

l: Proserpine, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having finished his tenth labour, £urystheus imposed anoAer
s: Proserpine was enchanted by the sweetness of Orpheus's music and allowed him to carry his dead wife back from hell. She later received Hercules kindly as her brother and allowed him to release Theseus and Pirithous from their chains.

l: Theseus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having finished his tenth labour, £urystheus imposed anoAer
s: Theseus carried away Antiope, or Hippolyte according to another account, and thereby incurred the hatred of the Amazons. He later led the Athenians against the Amazons in Attica and defeated them.

l: golden apples of the Hesperides, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having finished his tenth labour, £urystheus imposed anoAer
s: The golden apples of the Hesperides were the object of Hercules's last labour. The account says that some regarded them as actual golden apples guarded by a dragon, while others understood them poetically as the Hesperides' sheep.

l: Hesperides, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having finished his tenth labour, £urystheus imposed anoAer
s: The Hesperides were associated with a garden or country called Hesperis and were said by some mythologists to possess golden apples guarded by a dragon. Other accounts interpreted the golden apples as sheep or as their golden-colored fleeces.

l: sheep of the Hesperides, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having finished his tenth labour, £urystheus imposed anoAer
s: The sheep of the Hesperides were described by some writers as animals of exquisite beauty. They were poetically called golden apples, either because of their appearance or because their fleeces glittered like gold.

l: Atlas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having finished his tenth labour, £urystheus imposed anoAer
s: Atlas was the brother of Hesperus and the husband of Hesperis, by whom he had the daughters called the Atlantides and Hesperides. He studied astrology and possessed a curiously wrought sphere of the stars, which led to the story that he carried the whole world on his shoulders. After Hercules returned the abducted girls to him, Atlas assisted Hercules and taught him astrology.

l: Amazons, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having finished his tenth labour, £urystheus imposed anoAer
s: The Amazons gathered at the river Thermodon to avenge the losses they had suffered through Hercules. Allied with the Scythians, they marched into Europe and Attica, where Theseus defeated them; the survivors later went with the Scythians into Scythia.

l: Attica, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having finished his tenth labour, £urystheus imposed anoAer
s: Attica was invaded by the Amazons, who encamped at a place afterward called the Amazonian Field. Theseus and the Athenians defeated them there and drove the survivors out.

l: Antiope, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having finished his tenth labour, £urystheus imposed anoAer
s: Antiope was carried away captive by Theseus, according to one account, and was later taken by him to the battle against the Amazons. She fought bravely in defense of Theseus and died in the battle.

l: battle of Theseus and the Amazons, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having finished his tenth labour, £urystheus imposed anoAer
s: In the battle in Attica, Theseus led an army raised from the citizens against the Amazons. The Athenians won, killed some of the Amazons, and drove the rest from Attica; Antiope died while defending Theseus.

l: Sardinia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having finished his tenth labour, £urystheus imposed anoAer
s: Sardinia was the island where Hercules, following an oracle, established a colony governed by the sons of the Thespiadae under Iolaus. Its fertile and cultivated region later became a subject of conflict for the Carthaginians.

l: Iolaus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having finished his tenth labour, £urystheus imposed anoAer
s: Iolaus was Hercules's nephew, admiral, and companion in his expeditions. He led the Thespiadae colony to Sardinia, defeated the inhabitants, divided the most fertile region among the settlers, and later returned toward Greece and Sicily. The colonists honored him as a father and as a demi-god.

l: Thespiadae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having finished his tenth labour, £urystheus imposed anoAer
s: The Thespiadae were the fifty sons born to Hercules by the fifty daughters of Thespis. Most were sent with Iolaus to establish a colony in Sardinia, while two remained in Thebes and seven settled in the city of Thespis.

l: colony of the Thespiadae in Sardinia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having finished his tenth labour, £urystheus imposed anoAer
s: The colony of the Thespiadae in Sardinia was established under Iolaus after the settlers defeated the inhabitants and received the most fertile part of the island by lot. The colony became prosperous through cultivation, later mixed with barbarians, and eventually lived in inaccessible mountain places.

l: Omphale, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having finished his tenth labour, £urystheus imposed anoAer
s: Omphale was the daughter of Jardanus and queen of the Maeones. Hercules was sold as a slave to her after Apollo's oracle required his sale, but she later recognized his identity, freed him, and married him. Their son was Lamon.

l: Laomedon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having finished his tenth labour, £urystheus imposed anoAer
s: Laomedon, king of Troy, failed to give Hercules the horses he had promised for killing the whale. Hercules later attacked Troy, killed Laomedon and many of his men, and took the city.

l: Troy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having finished his tenth labour, £urystheus imposed anoAer
s: Troy was attacked and taken by Hercules because Laomedon had withheld the promised horses. Hercules killed many inhabitants, advanced Priam to the throne, and gave Hesione to Telamon.

l: Priam, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having finished his tenth labour, £urystheus imposed anoAer
s: Priam was the only son of Laomedon who opposed his father's refusal to deliver the horses to Hercules. After Hercules took Troy, he advanced Priam to his father's throne because of his justice.

l: Augeas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having finished his tenth labour, £urystheus imposed anoAer
s: Augeas defrauded Hercules of his promised reward. Hercules later invaded Elis, killed Augeas, took the city, and restored Phyleus to the kingdom because Phyleus had judged that the reward should be given to Hercules.

l: Sparta, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having finished his tenth labour, £urystheus imposed anoAer
s: Sparta was taken by Hercules after he defeated Hippocoon and his sons. Hercules restored Tyndarus to the Spartan kingdom on the condition that Tyndarus preserve it for his posterity.

l: Auge, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having finished his tenth labour, £urystheus imposed anoAer
s: Auge was the daughter of Aleus and secretly became pregnant by Hercules. Aleus ordered that she be drowned, but she was spared, sold to Teuthras, and eventually found her son Telephus.

l: Telephus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having finished his tenth labour, £urystheus imposed anoAer
s: Telephus was the son of Hercules and Auge. After Auge left him hidden on Mount Parthenius, shepherds found him being suckled by a hind and brought him to Corythus, who raised him. He later discovered his mother through an oracle, married Teuthras's daughter Agriopa, and became Teuthras's heir and successor.

l: Deianira, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having finished his tenth labour, £urystheus imposed anoAer
s: Deianira was the daughter of Oeneus. After Meleager had died, Hercules married her when he came to Calydon.

l: Meleager, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having finished his tenth labour, £urystheus imposed anoAer
s: Meleager was already dead when Hercules came to Calydon. After his death, Hercules married Deianira, the daughter of Oeneus.

l: Hercules's marriage to Deianira, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, Having finished his tenth labour, £urystheus imposed anoAer
s: Hercules's marriage to Deianira took place at Calydon after Meleager's death. Deianira was the daughter of Oeneus.

s: Meleager, son of Oeneus, joined many others in hunting the Calydonian boar and was the first to wound it. He gave the boar's skin to Atalanta, defended her against the sons of Thestius, and killed them when they refused to return it.

l: Oeneus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And here it will not be amiss to make a small digression, and de«
s: Oeneus sacrificed to all the gods except Diana after receiving a great plenty of corn. He was the father of Meleager and later received Periboea, whom Hipponous sent to him, as his wife; they had Tydeus.

s: The Calydonian boar was sent by Diana after Oeneus failed to sacrifice to her. It devastated the neighboring region and killed or destroyed much of the people's cattle before Meleager and the other hunters pursued it.

l: Calydonian boar hunt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And here it will not be amiss to make a small digression, and de«
s: The Calydonian boar hunt was undertaken by Meleager and many other notable hunters. Meleager first wounded the boar, and the hunters generally agreed that he should receive the boar's skin and the honor of the deed.

l: Atalanta, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And here it will not be amiss to make a small digression, and de«
s: Atalanta, daughter of Eclieneus, joined the Calydonian boar hunt. Meleager, who loved her, gave her the boar's skin and credited her with the glory, but the sons of Thestius later attacked her and took it by force.

l: Althea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And here it will not be amiss to make a small digression, and de«
s: Althea was Meleager's mother and the sister of the men he killed. She grieved excessively over their deaths, cursed Meleager, and wished the gods would destroy him; after his death she regretted her action and hanged herself.

l: Meleager's death, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And here it will not be amiss to make a small digression, and de«
s: Meleager was killed after Althea cursed him, and the gods heard her prayer. Another account says that his life depended on a firebrand preserved by Althea, which she threw into the fire after her brothers' deaths, thereby hastening his death.

l: Hercules, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And here it will not be amiss to make a small digression, and de«
s: Hercules diverted the river Achelous to benefit the Calydonians and assisted them against the Thesproti. He later fought several wars, killed Eurynonius accidentally, received the poisoned garment from Dejanira, died on Mount Oeta, and was believed to have been translated among the gods.

l: Achelous, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And here it will not be amiss to make a small digression, and de«
s: Achelous was diverted by Hercules into a channel that he cut, watering much of the Calydonian country and making it exceedingly fruitful. The account connects this work with the poetic story of Hercules fighting Achelous in the form of a bull and cutting off one of his horns.

l: Dejanira, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And here it will not be amiss to make a small digression, and de«
s: Dejanira was Hercules's wife. After learning of his love for Iole, she anointed his coat and shirt with the substance supplied by Nessus; when Hercules was dying from it, she recognized what she had done and hanged herself.

l: Nessus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And here it will not be amiss to make a small digression, and de«
s: Nessus was a centaur who carried travelers across the river Evenus for hire. He attempted to ravish Dejanira while carrying her across, and Hercules shot him; as he died, Nessus gave Dejanira instructions for preparing a substance intended to compel Hercules's love.

l: Nessus's love potion, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And here it will not be amiss to make a small digression, and de«
s: Nessus told Dejanira to mix his blood, oil, and some of his seed and use the mixture on Hercules's undergarment. Dejanira later applied the substance to Hercules's coat and shirt, believing it would preserve his love for her, but it acted as a destructive poison.

l: Iole, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And here it will not be amiss to make a small digression, and de«
s: Iole was the daughter of Eurytus. After Hercules defeated the sons of Eurytus for refusing to give her to him in marriage, he carried Iole away to the promontory of Cenaeum.

l: Hercules's poisoned garment, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And here it will not be amiss to make a small digression, and de«
s: Dejanira anointed Hercules's coat and shirt with the substance given by Nessus, and Lichas carried them to Hercules. When Hercules put them on, the poison spread through the garment, scorched his body, and caused intolerable torment.

l: Hercules's death, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, in Fifteen Books, And here it will not be amiss to make a small digression, and de«
s: After the poisoned garment caused his suffering, Hercules returned to Trachinia and sought an oracle's advice. He was carried to Mount Oeta, placed upon a funeral pile, and burned after Philoctetes set it alight; no bones were found, leading to the belief that he had been translated from humanity to the gods.

s: The unit states that Hercules went with the Argonauts on their expedition. It then announces that the account will proceed to treat of the Argonauts.

s: Jason, son of Æson and nephew of Pelias, leads an expedition of Argonauts aboard the Argo to Colchis to obtain the Golden Fleece. The Argonauts encounter Hesione, Phineus and his sons, and the hostile peoples of Pontus and Taurica before reaching Colchis. Medea, daughter of Æetes, helps Jason and the Argonauts escape, including by poisoning the dragon guarding the fleece, and Jason promises to marry her. After seizing the fleece, the Argonauts defeat pursuing Colchians and begin their return voyage, during which Glaucus foretells honors and future events.

s: Jason is described as the son of Æson and nephew of Pelias, ambitious to gain heroic fame. He leads the Argonaut expedition to Colchis, promises to marry Medea in return for her assistance, helps seize the Golden Fleece, and is wounded during the escape but later cured by Medea's remedies.
